2. Remarks/Discussion of Issues
Claims
By the present Amendment, claims 16-20 and 23-26 have been revised, and new claims 27-33 have been submitted for consideration. No new matter has been added. Claims 16-33 are pending in the application, which Applicant respectfully submits are in condition for allowance.
Interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) or § 112, Sixth Paragraph The Office Action asserts that "introduction element" in the claims should be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) or § 112, sixth paragraph. See Office Action, pp. 2- 4. Without acquiescing to the reasons for applying 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) or § 112, sixth paragraph, Applicant has revised the claims to remove the subject term. Accordingly, Applicants respectfully submit that the claims should not be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) or § 112, sixth paragraph.
Rejections under 35 U.S. C. § 112(a) or § 112, First Paragraph
The Office Action rejects claims 16-26 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) or § 112, first paragraph, as assertedly failing to comply with the written description requirement. See Office Action, pp. 4-5. Without acquiescing to the grounds of the rejections, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejections are moot in view of the revisions to the claims, and thus request withdrawal of the same.
Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) or § 112, Second Paragraph
The Office Action rejects claims 16-26 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) or § 112, second paragraph, as assertedly failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter Applicants regard as the invention. See Office Action, pp. 5-7. Without acquiescing to the grounds of the rejections, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejections are moot in view of the revisions to the claims, and thus request withdrawal of the same.
35 U.S.C. §101 Rejection
The Office Action rejects claims 16-26 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as assertedly being directed to non-statutory subject mater. See Office Action, p. 7-9. The Office Action asserts that the claims are directed to a judicial exception (mental process/mathematical process), and that the clams do not include additional elements that integrate the abstract ideal into a practical application, or amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.
Id. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.
According to the United States Supreme Court in Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l, 573 U.S. 208, 134 S. Ct. 2347, 110 USPQ2d 1976 (2014), the determination of whether a claim is directed to patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 comprises a two-part analysis. First, it must be determined whether the claim is directed to a "patent-ineligible concept" (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, or physical phenomena). Second, if the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept, it must be determined whether "an element or combination of elements that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself."' See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981.
The 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, United States Patent and Trademark Office (December 16, 2014), provides a two-part analysis, after an initial step of determining whether the claim is directed to a processes, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, regarding how the Office determines whether a claim is directed toward section 101 patent-eligible subject matter. Interim Eligibility Guidance, Federal Register/Vol. 79, No. 241/Tuesday, December 16, 2014/Rules and Regulations, p. 74621. Thus, after first determining the first step (Step 1) of whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, one must perform the two part Alice analysis: (A) Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), and (B) if an abstract idea is present in the claim, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself (Step 2B). See also MPEP
2106(III).
With regard to Step 1, under 35 U.S.C. § 101, there are four categories of subject matter eligible for patent protection: (1) processes; (2) machines; (3) manufactures; and (4) compositions of matter. Claims 16-23 and 26 are directed to machines or manufactures, and claims 24 and 25 are directed to processes, and therefore all claims fall within 35 U.S.C. § 101.
Step 2A addresses whether the method and article of manufacture are directed to an abstract idea. Notably, claims should not be deemed as being directed to an abstract idea simply because they are implemented using a computer. See, e.g., McRO, Inc. v.
Bandai Namco Games America Inc., 837 F.3d 1299, 1303 (Fed Cir. 2016) (Federal Circuit disposes of the general notion that computer implementation of a process is automatically a non-statutory, abstract idea, holding "that the ordered combination of claimed steps, using unconventional rules that relate sub-sequences of phonemes, timings, and morph weight sets, is not directed to an abstract idea and is therefore patent- eligible subject matter under § 101.").
According to the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Step 2A is further divided into two prongs for determining whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception, including abstract ideas. In Prong One, it is determined whether the claim recites a judicial exception, and with regard to an abstract idea in particular, whether the claim recites subject matter from one of three groupings: (a) mathematical concepts, (b) certain methods of organizing human activity-fundamental economic principles or practices, and (c) mental processes. "Claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas ...." See Federal Register / Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 53. If it is determined that the claim does recite a judicial exception, then the analysis proceeds to Prong Two of Step 2A. In Prong Two, it is determined whether the recited judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea) is integrated into a practical application of that judicial exception. Id.
With regard to Prong One, the revised guidance for analyzing patentable subject matter provides: "Claims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind, for instance when the human mind is not equipped to perform the claim limitations. See SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019) (declining to identify the claimed collection and analysis of network data as abstract because 'the human mind is not equipped to detect suspicious activity by using network monitors and analyzing network packets as recited by the claims')..." See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(III)(A) (emphasis added).
Similarly, claim 16, for example, is directed to a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled, and a memory storing instructions causing a computer to determine a set of curves defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, and reconstruct the cavity in response to the determined set of curves. These features can not be performed by the human mind. Applicant therefore respectfully submits that claim 16 is not directed to an abstract idea.
However, assuming arguendo that claim 1, recites at least one abstract idea, the question becomes whether that abstract idea is integrated into a practical application. "A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception." See Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 54 (emphasis added).
In the present Application, claim 16 integrates any potential abstract idea into at least the practical application reconstructing a cavity in response to the determined set of curves. This practical limitation prevents monopolization (improper pre-emption) of any potential abstract idea recited in claim 1, and therefore evidences a practical application of the same.
Another consideration indicative of an additional element integrating the judicial exception into a practical application is whether it reflects an improvement in the function of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field. Id. In this context, the claimed embodiments result in improvements in the field of medical imaging, where a cavity (e.g., heart) can be more quickly and effectively reconstructed using set of curves defined by a bendable segment of a catheter, as opposed to relying on points of contact by the distal tip of the catheter. The Specification identifies the technical problem addressed by the claimed subject matter as: "Since in an acceptable time only few different positions of the tip of the ablation catheter within the cavity can be determined, the reconstructed cavity, which is determined based on only these few locations of the tip of the ablation catheter, has a poor quality only." See Specification, p. 1, lines 14-17. See also p. 1, lines 20-23 ("It is an object of the present invention to provide a cavity determination apparatus, a cavity determination method and a cavity determination computer program for determining a cavity within an object, which allows determining the cavity within the object with improved quality in a relatively short time.") (emphasis added). Thus, claim 1 is directed to improvements in other technology or technical field.
In Thales Visionix v. USA and Elbit Systems, 2015-5150 (Fed. Cir. March 8, 2017), the Federal Circuit held that the claims at issue were patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, as a matter of law. In considering step one of the Alice analysis, "whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept," the Federal Circuit noted that "'all inventions at some level embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas.'... We must therefore ensure at step one that we articulate what the claims are directed to with enough specificity to ensure the step one inquiry is meaningful." Id. (citing Mayo, 566 U.S. at 71 (2012); Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2354 ("[W]e tread carefully in construing this exclusionary principle lest it swallow all of patent law.") (emphasis added).
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the claims also satisfy Prong Two in Step 2A of the analysis as set forth 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance. Therefore, the first part of the Alice analysis is satisfied, and the second part need not be addressed.
However, assuming arguendo that Step 2A has not been satisfied, Applicant proceeds to apply the second part of the Alice analysis (Step 2B). In accordance with Step 2B, Applicant submits that various elements in the claims are sufficient to ensure that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself, particularly in that the claims as a whole is for a particular application of the asserted abstract idea. See, e.g., Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 56 ("[I]f a claim has been determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2A, examiners should then evaluate the additional elements individually and in combination under Step 2B to determine whether they provide an inventive concept (i.e., whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the exception itself.").
For example, claim 1 recites inter alia a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled and comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements, and reconstructing the cavity in response to a determined set of curves from shape sensing information from the catheter. These practical applications amount to significantly more than any abstract idea to which the claim assertedly may otherwise be directed.
Accordingly, even assuming elements may involve abstract ideas, the claims are still directed to patent eligible subject matter due to application of the inventive concept. Applicant submits that the claims satisfy the second stage of the Alice Corp. test, and that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. See, e.g. Electric Power Group, LLC v. Alstom S.A., 830 F.3d 1350 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("Reflecting those points, we have described ... the second-stage inquiry (where reached) as looking more precisely at what the claim elements add-specifically, whether, in the Supreme Court's terms, they identify an "'inventive concept"' in the application of the ineligible matter to which (by assumption at stage two) the claim is directed." (citing Enfish, LLC v.
Microsoft Corp., 822 F.3d 1327, 1335-36 (Fed. Cir. 2016); Internet Patents Corp. v.
Active Network, Inc., 790 F.3d 1343, 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2015); Bascom GlobalInternet Servs., Inc. v. AT&TMobilityLLC, No. 2015-1763, 2016 WL 3514158, at *5 (Fed. Cir. June 27, 2016)).
Notably, the "inventive concept" that transforms the abstract idea into a patent- eligible invention "may arise in one or more of the individual claim limitations or in the ordered combination of the limitations," as discussed above. See BASCOM, at p. 13 (citing Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355) (emphasis added). In addition, as discussed above in the analysis under Prong Two of revised Step 2A, the claim features recite improvements in other technology or technical field. Again, such improvements amount to "significantly more" than the assertedly abstract idea itself, transforming the abstract idea into a patent- eligible application. See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (Syllabus at 3, Slip Op. at 15). See also BASCOM, p. 17 ("Thus, construed in favor of the nonmovant BASCOM the claims are 'more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the [abstract idea].' Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357. Instead, the claims may be read to "improve[] an existing technological process." Id. at 2358 (discussing the claims in Diehr, 450 U.S. 175)."). Accordingly, even assuming the claims are directed to abstract ideas, they still include patent eligible subject matter since they recite improvements to a technical field in accordance with the Alice analysis.
Accordingly, for at least the reasons set forth above, Applicant respectfully submits that the second part of the Alice test is also not satisfied, and therefore respectfully request withdrawal of the rejection of all pending claims under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
Rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 102 Rejection
Claims 16-26 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) as being anticipated by Barbagli et al. (U.S. Patent No. 2009/0076476). See Office Action, p. 9. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection at least for the reasons discussed below. Applicant's silence on certain aspects of the rejections is by no means a concession as to the propriety.
Claim 16
In rejecting claim 16, the Office Action asserts that "an introduction element for being introduced into the cavity" is disclosed by catheter 604, FIGs. 1, 8-10, 17-18; that "wherein the introduction element comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements" is disclosed by paras. [0055]-[0057], FIGs. 1, 8-10, 17-18; that "a curve determination device processor configured to determine a set of curves defined by the bendable segment" is disclosed by position determining system 70, paras. [0060], [0078], [0057]; that "wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements" is disclosed by FIG. 11, step 1114; that "and the determined set of curves comprises contact curves and non-contact curves" is disclosed by FIG. 11, steps 1116, 1118, 1120; that "the contact curves and non-contact curves not being distinguished from eash other by contact information;" is disclosed by FIG. 11; that "a cavity reconstruction device processor" is disclosed by 302, paras. [0072]-[0073]; and that "configured to reconstruct the cavity in response to the determined set of curves" is disclosed by FIG. 11, step 1122, paras. [0071]-[0072], [0080]. See Office Action, pp. 9-10.
Generally, Barbagli et al. is directed to a medical instrument system that includes a position determining system for determining the position of a distal end of a working instrument (e.g., a catheter), and a force sensor that generates force signals responsive to forces applied to the distal end portion of the working instrument to determine characteristics of tissue which the distal end contacts. See, e.g., Abstract, paras. [0011], [0013]. Although Barbagli et al. mentions shape sensing, it is only in the context of determining a position of the distal end of a catheter, and not for determining curves defined by a bendable segment of a catheter. See, e.g., paras. [0008], [0060], [0079]. For example, para. [0067] of Barbagli et al. provides inter alia: "[T]he computer assembly (6) is configured to receive and process the force signals from the force sensor system (34) and the position signals from the position determining system (70).... The computer assembly (6) is also configured to process the force signals and position signals to generate a geometric map of an area of body tissue correlated to the tissue compliance of the tissue or other characteristic of the body tissue related to its tissue compliance." (Emphasis added).
Accordingly, Barbagli et al. does not disclose at least a computer including a non- transitory storage medium for storing instructions that, when executed by the computer, cause the computer to determine a set of curves defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements, and reconstruct the cavity in response to the determined set of curves, as recited in claim 1, as amended.
Further, the Office Action cites to steps 1116, 1118 and 1120 of FIG. 11 of Barbagli et al. as assertedly disclosing the determined set of curves comprising contact curves and non-contact curves. However, these steps describe contact and non-contact of only the distal tip of a force sensing catheter with the surface of a cavity, not the contact and non-contact of curves of a catheter. Also, this contact/non-contact determination by Barbagli et al. is based on the extent of force applied to the distal tip, not shape sensing information. For example, Barbagli et al. provides: "Accordingly, a force reading above the force threshold may indicate that the tip of the force sensing catheter has pushed onto the surface of the cavity .... Furthermore, a force reading below the force threshold may indicate that the tip of the force sensing catheter may not be touching the surface of the cavity." See para. [0079].
Accordingly, Barbagli et al. also does not disclose at least a computer including a non-transitory storage medium for storing instructions that, when executed by the computer, cause the computer to determine a set of curves defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements, and wherein the determined set of curves comprises contact curves and non-contact curves.
For anticipation, there must be no difference between the claimed invention and the reference disclosure, as viewed by a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention. See, e.g., Scripps Clinic & Res. Found. v. Genentech, Inc., 927 F.2d 1565, 18 USPQ2d 1001 (Fed. Cir. 1991). Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that Barbagli et al. does not disclose each and every element of claim 16, and thus the rejection of claim 16 as being anticipated by Barbagli et al. under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) should be withdrawn.
Claims 24 and 26
Applicant respectfully submits that Barbagli et al. does not disclose each and every element of independent claims 24 and 26 at least for substantially the same reasons set forth above with regard to claim 16. Thus the rejection of claims 24 and 26 as being anticipated by Barbagli et al. under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) should be withdrawn.
Claims 17-23 and 25
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 17-23 and 25, and submit that these claims are allowable over the applied art at least because they depend from independent claims 16 and 24, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable, as well as in view of their additional recitations. Thus, withdrawal of the rejections of claims 17-23 and 25 is respectfully requested.
New claims
Applicant respectfully submits that new claims 27-33 are allowable over the applied art at least because they ultimately depend from independent claims 16 and 26, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable, as well as in view of their additional recitations.
Conclusion
In view of the foregoing explanations, Applicants respectfully request that the Examiner reconsider and reexamine the present application, allow claims 16-33, and pass the application to issue. In the event that there are any outstanding matters remaining in the present application, the Examiner is invited to contact Van C. Ernest (Reg. No. 44,099) at (571) 283.0720 to discuss these matters.
Respectfully submitted on behalf of:
Koninklijke Philips, N.V.
